author: fallintoplace
title: Bug: DevTools single-string console formatter consumes missing substitution arguments
text:
React version: Current main (`b685b40d`)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Call the DevTools helper with more substitution specifiers than arguments:

```js
formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString('%s %s', 'value');
formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString('%d %d', 1);
```

2. Observe the returned strings.

Link to code example:

https://github.com/react/react/blob/b685b40d9a719bee47422283fd86b5db2e4753ea/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils/index.js#L185-L233

## The current behavior

The helper shifts from an empty arguments array for the unmatched specifier, so it returns `value undefined` and `1 NaN`.

This helper is used to build the message key for warnings and errors logged during render, commit, and passive effects. As a result, DevTools can track a different message from the one produced by the console.

## The expected behavior

Unmatched specifiers should remain literal, matching browser console behavior and Node `util.format`:

```text
value %s
1 %d
```

The sibling `formatConsoleArguments` helper was updated with this behavior in #36930, but `formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString` still consumes a missing argument.

author: dai-shi
title: [Flight] Performance track debug info is not recovered for plain object roots
text:
## Summary

`flushComponentPerformance` reads `root._debugInfo` from the chunk. When
that array is empty and the chunk is fulfilled, it recovers the debug info
from the resolved value, but only when the value is an array, an async
iterable, a React element, or a lazy:

```js
if (debugInfo.length === 0 && root.status === 'fulfilled') {
  const resolvedValue = resolveLazy(root.value);
  if (
    typeof resolvedValue === 'object' && resolvedValue !== null &&
    (isArray(resolvedValue) ||
      typeof resolvedValue[ASYNC_ITERATOR] === 'function' ||
      resolvedValue.$$typeof === REACT_ELEMENT_TYPE ||
      resolvedValue.$$typeof === REACT_LAZY_TYPE) &&
    isArray(resolvedValue._debugInfo)
  ) {
    debugInfo = resolvedValue._debugInfo;
  }
}
```

A plain object root is excluded, so the Server Components track in the
Performance panel does not work for payloads whose root is a plain object,
even when the resolved value carries a `_debugInfo` array. Verified in
`react-server-dom-webpack@19.3.0-canary-28cd4bb0-20260723`.

## Context

Waku's RSC payload root is a plain object mapping slot ids to elements
(`Record<string, unknown>`), which lets one payload carry several named
elements. This shape is deliberate and we would like to keep it. Today we
patch the read site with a build transform that drops the type restriction,
which works but is coupled to the compiled output:

https://github.com/wakujs/waku/blob/main/packages/waku/src/lib/vite-plugins/patch-rsdw.ts

@vitejs/plugin-rsc documents the same shape constraint for its performance
track example (vitejs/vite-plugin-react#1152, vitejs/vite-plugin-react#1304).

## Request

Relax the recovery to accept any object value that carries an own
`_debugInfo` array. The type restriction seems to mirror
`moveDebugInfoFromChunkToInnerValue`, where it guards attaching
`_debugInfo` to the value. The read site only reads the property, so the
restriction does not appear to protect anything there, and the relaxation
is additive: values without `_debugInfo` behave as before.

If there is a supported way to get the performance track with a plain
object root without reshaping the payload, that guidance would also
resolve this for us.

author: joewalker
title: Bug: Importing `react-dom/server` under Deno prevents the process from ever exiting.
text:
Deno's export-condition resolution selects the **browser** server build, which creates a `MessageChannel` at module scope and assigns `port1.onmessage`. That refs the port against the event loop, and nothing ever closes it, so the runtime stays alive forever after the script finishes.

No rendering is required, because the channel is created at module scope. The equivalent Node import is unaffected, since `server.node.js` schedules on `setImmediate` and contains no `MessageChannel`.

React version: 19.2.8

(Tested against Deno 2.9.3 and Node 26.5.0)

## Steps To Reproduce

Setup `npm install react-dom@19.2.8`

- Case 1. `node -e "import 'react-dom/server'; console.log('done');"`
- Case 2. `deno eval "import 'react-dom/server'; console.log('done');"`
- Case 3. `deno eval "import 'react-dom/server.node'; console.log('done');"`

In all cases "done" is output.

However, under node (case 1), the process completes. Under deno, using 'react-dom/server' (case 2), the process hangs. Under deno, using 'react-dom/server.node' (case 3), the process completes.

## Is this a deno bug?

TL;DR: Not really, both node and deno act the same when given the same builds.

`react-dom`'s `./server` export map points the `deno` condition to the browser export:

```json
"./server": {
  "react-server": "./server.react-server.js",
  "workerd":      "./server.edge.js",
  "bun":          "./server.bun.js",
  "deno":         "./server.browser.js",
  "worker":       "./server.browser.js",
  "node":         "./server.node.js",
  "edge-light":   "./server.edge.js",
  "browser":      "./server.browser.js",
  "default":      "./server.node.js"
}
```

(Note that deno also sets the `node` condition, however the `deno` condition is listed first above so it wins)

Neither Deno nor react-dom misbehaves alone; it is specifically Deno resolving to the browser build.

The key difference between the builds is the construction of `MessageChannel`.

`cjs/react-dom-server.browser.production.js:132` says:

```javascript
var channel = new MessageChannel(),
  taskQueue = [];
channel.port1.onmessage = function () {
  var task = taskQueue.shift();
  task && task();
};
```

(The repro loads the development build, as NODE_ENV is unset - same logic at `cjs/react-dom-server.browser.development.js:8818`, just formatted differently.)

This is module-scope state with no teardown path, so the port stays open and ref'd for the lifetime of the module. In a browser that is invisible - there is no process to exit. In any runtime with an exit condition, it pins the process open.

`cjs/react-dom-server.node.production.js` doesn't do the same.


### Reduced, with no React dependency at all

The following hangs:

```sh
deno eval "const c = new MessageChannel(); c.port1.onmessage = () => {}; console.log('done');"
```

Removing the handler assignment makes it exit 0:

```sh
deno eval "const c = new MessageChannel(); console.log('done');"
```

Constructing a `MessageChannel` is inert, but assigning a handler starts the port and refs it. This reduction also hangs under Node, so the underlying behaviour is not Deno-specific - Deno merely loads the build that does it.

The solution could be to point deno at a node build (which works in my testing) or maybe to have the browser build's scheduler `unref()` the port where available, or create the channel lazily on first `scheduleWork` and close it when the task queue drains, so an import with no render leaves nothing open.

author: narukeu
title: With Node.js now offering solid support for require(esm), I suggest React consider a pure ESM build for its next major release.
text:
With Node.js now offering solid support for require(esm), I suggest React consider a pure ESM build for its next major release.

Currently, React’s primary build artifacts published to npm are still based on CommonJS. Historically, retaining CommonJS made practical sense for compatibility, as a vast number of Node.js tooling and server-side applications rely on synchronous `require()` to load React.

But today, newer versions of Node.js can synchronously load ESM modules via `require()`, the fundamental blocker preventing React from migrating to a pure ESM build has essentially disappeared.

Therefore, I believe a pure ESM build for React is now practically viable in the next major version, and I encourage the React team to evaluate this direction. Given that a new major release would likely bump the minimum Node.js runtime requirement as well, this might be the perfect timing to push forward with a pure ESM build.

author: filiptrivan
title: Bug: 19.2 batched Suspense reveal can consume the wrong completion segment when a resumed (PPR) stream reuses a queued segment id — DOM corruption + hydration failure
text:
## Summary

Since React 19.2's batched Suspense reveal ("Batching Suspense Boundaries for SSR streaming"), the inline `completeBoundary` runtime (`$RC`) no longer consumes its content segment synchronously — it queues `(boundary, content)` pairs into `$RB` and consumes them in a deferred `revealCompletedBoundaries` (`$RV`) flush (rAF, then a ~300ms/2.3s-LCP throttle). The queued content segment `<div hidden id="S:n">` therefore **stays in the DOM with its id until the flush**.

In a prerender+resume (PPR) document, the resume stream's segment ids are allocated independently of the prerender's, so a resume segment can legally reuse an id the shell already used for a boundary completion — one document containing two `<div hidden id="S:4">` (the shell boundary `B:4`'s completion segment, and the resume segment feeding postponed hole `P:4` via `$RS("S:4","P:4")`). This was safe pre-19.2 **by ordering**: each segment was consumed and removed synchronously by its own inline script before the next same-id segment parsed.

With batching, when the whole document is parsed in one burst (CDN cache hit / fast network / busy main thread delaying rAF), the parser executes `$RS("S:4","P:4")` while the shell's `S:4` is still queued and in the DOM. `completeSegment`'s `document.getElementById("S:4")` returns the **first (wrong) segment** and moves the wrong subtree into the resume hole. The subsequent `$RV` flush then operates on a cross-linked tree and throws:

```
HierarchyRequestError: Failed to execute 'insertBefore' on 'Node': The new child element contains the parent.
```

leaving orphaned never-consumed hidden segments, after which hydration fails (`Minified React error #418` storm — observed 7–38 per load) and React discards the SSR output and client-renders. In the worst observed case the boundary's fallback had already been deleted when the insert threw, leaving a blank region and a pegged main thread (user-facing "Page Unresponsive").

## Environment

- react-dom `19.2.3` (vendored by Next.js `16.2.9`, `cacheComponents: true`, deployed on Vercel — the shell+resume document form)
- Observed on a production e-commerce storefront; browsers: Chromium (headless and desktop), Brave.

## Reproduction

On a captured shell+resume document containing the duplicate-id shape (two `<div hidden id="S:4">` + `$RS("S:4","P:4")` later in the stream):

1. Serve the bytes to the browser **in one burst** (e.g. Playwright `route.fulfill` with the fully buffered body — the deterministic form of a CDN cache-hit delivery).
2. Stock 19.2.3 inline runtime: **10/10 runs corrupt** — instrumented `document.getElementById` shows the `S:4` lookup running with 2 matches present and returning index 0 (the shell's queued segment); then the `HierarchyRequestError` from `$RV`, orphaned `div[hidden][id^="S:"]` nodes, and the #418 storm.
3. Replace **only** the inline `$RC` template with the pre-19.2-style synchronous equivalent (same per-pair logic `$RV` runs — fallback walk, child move, `"$"` reveal, `_reactRetry` — applied at script-execution time): **0/10 corrupt**, all segments consumed, clean hydration.

Over a real network the failure is timing-dependent (~2/3 of hard loads on a fast connection in our measurements; a dribbled stream lets the rAF flush win the race), which is why it presents as a flaky production-only hydration failure.

I'm happy to provide the captured HTML documents, the instrumentation snippets, and to work on a minimal standalone repro if useful.

## Suggested direction

Resumed streams' segment/placeholder ids must not be able to collide with ids the shell's queued completions still hold in the DOM. Options that would each fix it:

- distinct id namespace (or prefix) for resume segments, or
- `completeSegment` (`$RS`) flushing the pending `$RB` queue before its lookup, or
- boundary completions removing the queued segment from the id space at queue time (e.g. clearing its `id` when pushed to `$RB`).

## Note

Filed with a cross-reference in vercel/next.js, since the colliding document shape is produced by Next's PPR prerender+resume path, but the ordering regression itself is in the 19.2 fizz inline runtime.

author: AntonyDugler
title: Bug: infinite synchronous loop in getParentHydrationBoundary during event dispatch when <html> is rendered inside a container div (jsdom + portaled focus content)
text:
## Summary

`react-dom` enters an **infinite synchronous loop** inside the event-dispatch path — `getClosestInstanceFromNode` → `getParentHydrationBoundary` → repeated `previousSibling` walking — when:

1. the rendered tree contains an `<html>` element **nested inside a container `<div>`** (the default React Testing Library mount, under jsdom), and
2. an event is dispatched that involves portaled content with focus guards (e.g. opening a Radix UI dialog, or pointer/focus events after such content has existed in the document).

Because the loop is synchronous microtask/dispatch work, it never yields: the test runner's timeouts never fire and the process spins at 100% CPU indefinitely. Where it strikes is nondeterministic across runs (whichever event dispatch first hits the walk), which makes it look like flaky "hanging tests".

## Reproduction (18 lines, vitest + jsdom)

```tsx
import * as Dialog from "@radix-ui/react-dialog";
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

describe("nested-html repro", () => {
  it("hangs forever on the click", async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(
      <html lang="en">
        <body>
          <Dialog.Root>
            <Dialog.Trigger>open</Dialog.Trigger>
            <Dialog.Portal>
              <Dialog.Overlay />
              <Dialog.Content>
                <Dialog.Title>Hello</Dialog.Title>
                <button>inside</button>
              </Dialog.Content>
            </Dialog.Portal>
          </Dialog.Root>
        </body>
      </html>,
    );
    await user.click(screen.getByText("open")); // ← never returns
    expect(await screen.findByRole("dialog")).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});
```

Remove the `<html>`/`<body>` wrapper (render the dialog directly into the container) and the same test passes in ~600 ms.

## Observed spinning stack

Captured by pausing the hung worker under the V8 inspector (`kill -USR1` + `Debugger.pause`); 100% of samples over multiple seconds sit in this loop:

```
get previousSibling
getParentHydrationBoundary        (react-dom-client.development.js)
getClosestInstanceFromNode
dispatchEventForPluginEventSystem
dispatchDiscreteEvent
[jsdom] innerInvokeEventListeners / _dispatch
fireFocusEventWithTargetAdjustment
[Radix FocusScope] focusFirst → patched focus
commitHookEffectListMount          (FocusScope's mount effect)
commitPassiveMountOnFiber
```

A related manifestation: after any render of such a nested-`<html>` tree has been mounted and unmounted, a **subsequent** `user.type()`/pointer interaction in the same jsdom document can enter the same walk via `dispatchContinuousEvent`, again never returning.

## Why this shape occurs in the wild

Frameworks whose root component renders the full document shell (`<html><head/><body>…`) — e.g. TanStack Start, and similar SSR document-root apps — hit this whenever tests mount the real root via React Testing Library's default container `<div>`. React warns `In HTML, <html> cannot be a child of <div>` (fair), but the failure mode is an unkillable synchronous hang rather than an error, and it strikes probabilistically at whichever event dispatch comes next.

**Workaround** that resolved it for us: create the root on `document` itself (`createRoot(document)`), so the rendered `<html>` becomes the real `documentElement`. It would still be worth `getParentHydrationBoundary` guarding against non-terminating walks (or React turning the invalid-nesting warning into a hard error) so the invalid case fails loudly instead of spinning forever.

## Environment

- react / react-dom **19.2.5**
- jsdom **29.1.1** (vitest **4.1.10**, `environment: "jsdom"`)
- @testing-library/react **16.3.2**, @testing-library/user-event **14.6.1**
- @radix-ui/react-dialog **1.1.15**
- node **v24.17.0**, macOS 15 (also reproduced on ubuntu-latest CI)

author: dai-shi
title: [Flight] Let encodeFormAction reuse the default encoding
text:
## Summary

This is a follow-up to #27563.

The SSR Flight client's `encodeFormAction` callback fully replaces React's default form action encoding. A framework cannot call the default encoder and change only one field.

A common use case is changing the form action URL while keeping the default encoding, so `decodeAction` still works. For example, a framework may add a query parameter that identifies a no-JS action request without reading the request body.

Today, frameworks must copy React's encoding behavior using public APIs. This includes serializing the arguments, renaming fields, generating prefixes, caching results, and handling suspension. The callback also does not receive `identifierPrefix` or a stable identity for unbound references.

This logic now exists in two implementations:

* waku: https://github.com/wakujs/waku/pull/2191
* `@vitejs/plugin-rsc`: https://github.com/vitejs/vite-plugin-react/pull/1280

## Proposal

Pass a bound default encoder to the callback:

```ts
encodeFormAction?: (
  id: string,
  args: Promise<unknown[]>,
  encodeDefault: () => ReactCustomFormAction,
) => ReactCustomFormAction;
```

A framework could then write:

```ts
const encodeFormAction = (id, args, encodeDefault) => ({
  ...encodeDefault(),
  action: currentUrl + '?my-marker=1',
});
```

React would keep control of caching, prefixes, and suspension, while frameworks could change only the fields they need.

Exporting `defaultEncodeFormAction` would not solve this by itself because React must bind the reference state and provide the Fizz `identifierPrefix`.

## `useActionState` permalink

When `permalink` is set, Fizz applies it after `encodeFormAction` and replaces the callback's action URL.

Applying the permalink before the callback, or adding a final action transform, would let frameworks preserve their URL changes.

author: HoneyTyagii
title: Build: Inject the runtime React version from ReactVersions.js
text:
## Summary

Use `ReactVersions.js` as the single source of truth for React's runtime version and inject that value during the build.

## Current behavior

`packages/shared/ReactVersion.js` currently hard-codes the React version:

```js
export default '19.3.0';
```

The file contains a TODO explaining that the version should instead be injected during the build from `ReactVersions.js`.

This creates multiple version values that must be updated together, including:

- `ReactVersions.js`
- `packages/shared/ReactVersion.js`
- Package metadata such as `packages/react/package.json`

A missed update could cause runtime version information, release metadata, and DevTools compatibility handling to disagree.

## Proposed change

1. Add a build-time version token or equivalent injection mechanism.
2. Source the injected value from `ReactVersions.js`.
3. Update `packages/shared/ReactVersion.js` to use the injected value, or remove the module if its consumers can be migrated safely.
4. Ensure source-mode tests and local development receive a deterministic version.
5. Cover stable, canary, and experimental release channels.
6. Add validation that detects divergence between emitted runtime metadata and canonical release metadata.

The existing Rollup constant replacement stage in `scripts/rollup/build.js` may provide a suitable integration point.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ReactVersions.js` is the only manually maintained source for the core React release version.
- Stable builds expose the canonical React version at runtime.
- Canary and experimental builds expose their expected release-channel version formats.
- Source tests, watch builds, production builds, and release builds do not contain an unresolved version token.
- DevTools version compatibility behavior continues to work.
- CI reports a clear failure if runtime and canonical release metadata diverge.
- The obsolete TODO and duplicate runtime version constant are removed.

## Additional context

Relevant source locations:

- `packages/shared/ReactVersion.js`
- `ReactVersions.js`
- `scripts/rollup/build.js`
- `packages/react/package.json`


<!--
  Please provide a CodeSandbox (https://codesandbox.io/s/new), a link to a
  repository on GitHub, or provide a minimal code example that reproduces the
  problem. You may provide a screenshot of the application if you think it is
  relevant to your bug report. Here are some tips for providing a minimal
  example: https://stackoverflow.com/help/mcve.
-->

## The current behavior

On iOS (Expo dev runtime / Metro bundler), invoking a Server Function from a `React.Suspense` boundary throws:

```
ERROR [Error: Uncaught (in promise, id: 0) ReferenceError: Property '__webpack_get_script_filename__' doesn't exist]

Call Stack
  resolveModuleChunk (node_modules/react-server-dom-webpack/cjs/react-server-dom-webpack-client.browser.development.js:1607:34)
  model.then$argument_0 (node_modules/react-server-dom-webpack/cjs/react-server-dom-webpack-client.browser.development.js:2771:38)
```

**Regression boundary:** Pinning all three packages to **19.1.8** resolves the issue. The Server Function completes and `Hello, World!` renders.

## The expected behavior

The Server Function should resolve and successfully render `Hello, World!` on iOS, as it does with `react-server-dom-webpack@19.1.8`.

---

## Root cause analysis

The regression is in **`react-server-dom-webpack`**, not `react` or `react-dom`. A diff of `react-server-dom-webpack-client.browser.development.js` between 19.1.8 and 19.2.0 is in `investigation/rsdw-client-browser.diff`.

### What changed in 19.2.0

`resolveModuleChunk()` was rewritten to collect **debug/IO tracing metadata** for each webpack chunk referenced by a resolved client module. It now calls a **new Webpack runtime global** that does not exist in 19.1.8:

```js
var scriptFilename = __webpack_get_script_filename__(chunkId);
```

This symbol appears **exactly once** in the entire 19.2.0 package tree — at line 1607 of `react-server-dom-webpack-client.browser.development.js`.

### 19.1.8 — `resolveModuleChunk` (12 lines, no filename lookup)

```js
function resolveModuleChunk(chunk, value) {
  if ("pending" === chunk.status || "blocked" === chunk.status) {
    var resolveListeners = chunk.value,
      rejectListeners = chunk.reason;
    chunk.status = "resolved_module";
    chunk.value = value;
    chunk.reason = null;
    null !== resolveListeners &&
      (initializeModuleChunk(chunk),
      wakeChunkIfInitialized(chunk, resolveListeners, rejectListeners));
  }
}
```

### 19.2.0 — `resolveModuleChunk` (~70 lines, requires Webpack global)

```js
function resolveModuleChunk(response, chunk, value) {
  if ("pending" === chunk.status || "blocked" === chunk.status) {
    releasePendingChunk(response, chunk);
    value = value[1];  // chunk preload manifest from client reference metadata
    for (var debugInfo = [], i = 0; i < value.length; ) {
      var chunkId = value[i++];
      value[i++];
      var scriptFilename = __webpack_get_script_filename__(chunkId);  // ← throws on Metro
      href = new URL(scriptFilename, document.baseURI).href;
      // builds ioInfo via performance.getEntriesByType("resource"), fake stacks, etc.
      chunkIOInfoCache.set(chunkId, ioInfo);
      target.push({ awaited: ioInfo });
    }
    chunk._debugInfo.push.apply(chunk._debugInfo, debugInfo);
    initializeModuleChunk(chunk);
  }
}
```

### Supporting infrastructure added in 19.2.0

| Addition | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `chunkIOInfoCache` | Caches per-chunk IO timing/size debug info |
| `resolveChunkDebugInfo()` | Attaches awaited IO info to chunks |
| `releasePendingChunk()` | Refactored chunk lifecycle |
| `initializeDebugChunk()` | Debug model chunk initialization |

Client file grew from **2,837 → 4,973 lines** (+75%).

### Why 19.1.8 works on non-Webpack runtimes

19.1.8 uses webpack globals that Expo/Metro already polyfills:

- `__webpack_require__`
- `__webpack_chunk_load__`
- `__webpack_require__.u` (with `chunkMap` fallback)

But it **never** calls `__webpack_get_script_filename__`, so the missing global is never hit.

### Call path

```
app/index.tsx
  React.Suspense → renderInfo() server function
    → RSC payload streamed back with client module reference
      → resolveModule() in react-server-dom-webpack client
        → resolveModuleChunk(response, chunk, clientReference)
          → __webpack_get_script_filename__(chunkId)  // ReferenceError
```

## Environment

| Component | Version |
|-----------|---------|
| Expo SDK | 57.0.6 |
| expo-router | 57.0.6 |
| react / react-dom / react-server-dom-webpack | 19.2.0 (broken) / 19.1.8 (works) |
| React Native | 0.86.0 |
| Node.js | v26.4.0 |
| Xcode | 26.6 (Build 17F113) |
| iOS Simulator | iPhone 17 Pro |

## Suggested fixes

1. **Guard the call in `react-server-dom-webpack`:** Check `typeof __webpack_get_script_filename__ === 'function'` before calling; fall back to `__webpack_require__.u(chunkId)` or skip IO debug info when absent.
2. **Expo/Metro shim:** Polyfill `__webpack_get_script_filename__` to return chunk URLs (similar to the existing `__webpack_require__.u` shim).

## Additional context

- Repro follows [Expo's RSC guide](https://docs.expo.dev/guides/server-components/) with `experiments.reactServerFunctions: true`
- No patches, shims, or workarounds in the repro — the failure is a direct integration issue between `react-server-dom-webpack@19.2.0` and Metro's partial Webpack runtime emulation

```ts
const selectedNode = nodes.find(n => n.id === selection?.node.id);
```

```js
if ($[0] !== nodes || $[1] !== selection?.node) {
```

- Add an unrelated read _after_ the declaration.
```ts
const selectedNode = nodes.find(n => n.id === selection?.node.id);
selection?.node.id; // <-- here
```
- Observe that the compiled out now caches on `selection?.node.id`
```js
if ($[0] !== nodes || $[1] !== selection?.node.id) {
```

**With manual memoization**
When using manual memoization, adhering to the rules enforced by the `exhaustive-deps` linting rule, this results in skipped compilation:

- Define a memo that uses an optional chain, e.g.:

```ts
const selectedNode = useMemo(
  () => nodes.find(n => n.id === selection?.node.id),
  [ nodes, selection?.node.id ]
);
```
- Observe that compilation is _skipped_.
- Add an unrelated read _after_ the memo
```ts
const selectedNode = useMemo(
  () => nodes.find(n => n.id === selection?.node.id),
  [ nodes, selection?.node.id ]
);
selection?.node.id; // <-- here
```
- Observe that the component now compiles, and the original memo is cached using `selection?.node.id`.

In both cases, adding the read _before_ the memoized code does not have an impact.

**Further notes:**
I was hoping for the compiler to understand the optional chain, in line with the `exhaustive-deps` lint rule. I _think_ that issue was reported before, including the workaround of extracting the chained variable outside of the memo.

Upon further investigation, I was happily surprised that the compiler does seem to be able to figure out the pattern! It's just the way to trigger it that seems unintentional. I hope this report helps the work towards fully supporting the compilation of these optional chaining patterns.

If there's anything else I can do to help, please let me know.

author: identy
title: Transient DOM duplication window (~300 ms) when batched Suspense reveal races hydration-time client render of dehydrated boundaries (React 19.2)
text:
**Summary**

Since React 19.2, two documented behaviors interact to produce a transient window where
streamed Suspense content exists twice in the DOM:

1. **Batched/throttled Suspense reveals** (React 19.2 blog): when `$RC(...)` executes for a
   streamed segment, the reveal may be queued for ~300 ms instead of applying immediately.
2. **Client-rendering dehydrated boundaries on document load** (#31620): if the
   document finishes loading and hydration finds a Suspense boundary still "dehydrated
   pending", React client-renders it from the flight payload.

When both fire on the same boundary — reveal queued at t≈75 ms, document load + hydration at
t≈100 ms — the client render mounts a **visible** copy while the streamed segment
(`<div hidden id="S:0">…`) remains unconsumed in the DOM. Both copies coexist until the queued
reveal batch runs (~300 ms after `$RC`), finds the boundary already resolved, and deletes the
orphaned segments.

**Impact**

- End users: none observed — the extra copy is `hidden` (excluded from the accessibility
  tree) and self-cleans within ~300 ms.
- Tooling: any DOM-wide query during the window sees duplicates. Playwright strict-mode
  aborts immediately on the violation (no retry), producing persistent flaky failures for
  any assertion issued right after `page.goto()` to a streamed route. This bit us across
  ~27 spec files until we adopted `.filter({ visible: true })` everywhere (the mitigation
  the Next.js team recommends in vercel/next.js#86577 for the Activity/cacheComponents
  variant — which we do NOT use; our app has neither).

**Reproduction (deterministic, production build)**

Environment: Next.js 16.2.x (App Router), React 19.2.x, a route with `loading.tsx` whose RSC
payload streams after the shell (any data-bound page works).

1. `next build && next start`.
2. Warm the server (visit the route once) — a warm server makes hydration consistently win
   the race against the queued reveal. Cold servers rarely reproduce (hydration arrives after
   the reveal executed), which disguises the issue as a "flaky test under load".
3. Load the route with a `MutationObserver` installed at document-start; observe:
   - t≈62–77 ms: segments arrive into `<div hidden id="S:0">`; `$RC("B:0","S:0")` executes but
     the reveal is queued;
   - t≈103 ms: document load → hydration client-renders the pending boundary → second, visible
     copy appears;
   - t≈103–373 ms: both copies present (all test ids ×2; one copy under `[hidden]`);
   - t≈373 ms (300 ms after `$RC`): queued batch runs, orphaned segments are deleted.
4. Raw server HTML contains each node exactly once (verified via direct fetch) — the
   duplication is client-side; there is no hydration mismatch logged.

**Expected**

Either the queued reveal is cancelled/flushed synchronously when hydration decides to
client-render the boundary, or the client render consumes/removes the streamed segment
immediately — so the DOM never holds both copies.

**Notes**

- We could not find an existing issue describing this exact interaction (reveal batching ×
  document-load client render). Happy to provide the full MutationObserver traces and a
  minimal repo if useful.
- Related (different trigger, same symptom family): vercel/next.js#86577.

## Structural duplicates in React codebase (34.1% of .ts/.tsx files affected)

I ran [find-duplicates](https://github.com/DecSec2030/find-duplicates) — a tool that detects structural code duplicates (normalizing identifiers, strings, and whitespace before comparing) — on the main branch at `c0c39a6`.

### Summary

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| .ts/.tsx files scanned | 521 |
| Files with duplicates | 178 (34.1%) |
| Duplicate groups | 342 |
| Duplicated blocks | 973 |

### By directory

| Directory | Duplicates | Files |
|-----------|-----------|-------|
| `compiler/packages/` | 816 | 165 |
| `packages/eslint-plugin-react-hooks/` | 85 | 6 |
| `compiler/scripts/` | 64 | 5 |
| `packages/react/` | 6 | 1 |
| `fixtures/` | 2 | 1 |

### Notable findings

**1. `compiler/packages/snap/src/minimize.ts` — 30 near-identical generator methods (142 duplicates)**

Functions like `removeStatements`, `removeCallArguments`, `removeFunctionParameters`, `simplifyCallExpressions`, etc. all follow the exact same pattern: count AST nodes of a type → loop with clone → traverse → replace. This is the single largest source of duplication.

**2. `compiler/scripts/ts-compile-fixture.ts` — 14 identical pipeline passes (64 duplicates)**

Each pipeline pass checks `if (env.hasErrors()) { return formatEnvError(...); }` with near-identical structure across all passes.

**3. `compiler/packages/babel-plugin-react-compiler/` — scattered scope/binding checks (15 files)**

A pattern of checking bindings and scope ranges (`if (binding) { ... }`) is repeated across 15 different files in the compiler, suggesting a candidate for a shared utility.

**4. Core `packages/react/` is clean — only 6 duplicate blocks in 1 file.**

The mature React core has very few structural duplicates, which is expected for a well-refactored codebase.

### Context

The vast majority of duplicates are in `compiler/` (React Forget), a newer, actively-developed package. The core React packages are essentially clean.

### Options

- `compiler/packages/snap/src/minimize.ts` — could extract a `createGenerator(pattern)` helper to eliminate the 30 repeated method bodies
- Pipeline passes — could use a higher-order function for the `hasErrors()` check
- Shared binding helpers — consolidate the scattered pattern into `Utils/binding.ts`

author: BranZhang
title: [Compiler Bug]: MobX observer component is compiled without an incompatible-library diagnostic and loses reactivity
text:
### What kind of issue is this?

- [x] React Compiler core (the JS output is incorrect, or your app works incorrectly after optimization)
- [ ] babel-plugin-react-compiler (build issue installing or using the Babel plugin)
- [ ] eslint-plugin-react-hooks (build issue installing or using the eslint plugin)
- [ ] react-compiler-healthcheck (build issue installing or using the healthcheck script)

### Link to repro

https://github.com/BranZhang/react-compiler-mobx-repro

### Repro steps

## Summary

When `babel-plugin-react-compiler` is enabled with `compilationMode: 'infer'`, a MobX `observer` component declared as a top-level function and then wrapped with `observer(Component)` can keep returning stale JSX after observable changes.

The failure is silent: no runtime error or compiler warning is shown. The UI keeps rendering the initial value after the MobX store changes.

## Reproduction

Repository: https://github.com/BranZhang/react-compiler-mobx-repro

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open `http://localhost:5199`, then click `store.increment()` three times.

## Actual Behavior

The rows using a top-level function declaration wrapped by `observer(...)` keep displaying `0`:

- `plain observer: 0`
- `observer + console.log: 0`

The MobX store value does change, and other subscribers can observe the updated value.

## Expected Behavior

The observed component should continue to update when `COUNTER_STORE.count` changes, or React Compiler should skip this pattern / warn that it is unsafe.

## Control Cases

The same reproduction includes several control cases:

- `observer + window write` updates to `3`, because the render-time global assignment makes React Compiler bail out.
- `observer + 'use no memo'` updates to `3`, because the component is skipped by React Compiler.
- `reaction + useState` updates to `3`, because it uses an explicit MobX subscription instead of render-time `observer` tracking.
- Commenting out `babel-plugin-react-compiler` in `vite.config.ts` makes all rows update correctly.
- Changing `const Plain = observer(PlainComponent)` to an inline function expression passed to `observer(...)` also makes the row update correctly.

## Suspected Mechanism

`observer` relies on executing the component function during render inside a MobX tracking context. Observable reads that actually happen during render become the component subscription.

The compiled output shows that `COUNTER_STORE.count` is still read on every render, so MobX continues tracking the observable and notifying the component. However, React Compiler caches the JSX created during the initial render without treating the observable value as a dependency. After a store update:

1. MobX triggers a re-render.
2. The component reads the latest `COUNTER_STORE.count`, so the MobX subscription remains active.
3. The compiled memo cache returns the JSX created during the initial render.
4. The component therefore keeps displaying the initial value even though it continues to re-render with updated observable values.

## Versions

- react: 19.2.0
- react-dom: 19.2.0
- mobx: 6.13.3
- mobx-react: 9.2.2
- mobx-react-lite: 4.1.1
- babel-plugin-react-compiler: 1.0.0
- vite: 5.4

author: inxx
title: Page hangs forever at 100% CPU inside the Fizz batched-reveal runtime (`$RV`) — `insertBefore` loop never terminates (React 19.2, reproduces in both Chrome and Safari)
text:
On a production e-commerce page rendered with streaming SSR (Next.js App Router + PPR, ~15 streamed Suspense boundaries), the browser main thread intermittently locks up **forever** during page load: 100% CPU, memory growing to multiple GBs, page stays blank/white. The renderer never returns to the event loop (Chrome DevTools cannot even attach/evaluate). We captured the exact location twice, in two different engines — see **The current behavior** below.

React version: 19.2.4 (vendored by Next.js 16.2.6, App Router, PPR enabled, `cacheComponents`). Also reproduced with the runtime shipped in Next 16.2.10 (byte-identical `$RV`).

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Serve a streaming-SSR page: Next.js App Router with PPR enabled, ~15 streamed Suspense boundaries, large SSR DOM (~1,700 nodes), and third-party scripts with active MutationObservers on the page.
2. Load the page under production-like server latency and reload repeatedly during an affected period — within ~10 reloads the main thread locks at 100% CPU, memory climbs to multiple GBs, and the page stays blank/white.

The hang is timing-dependent (segment arrival order/batching): repro rate on the same build swings between 0% and ~90% across hours, apparently tracking server response latency.

Link to code example:

No minimal repro yet — the hang depends on segment arrival timing/batching, so it does not isolate into a static sandbox. Happy to share the production URL **privately**, run instrumented builds/patches, and capture more traces (we can reproduce within ~10 reloads during affected periods). Guidance on what to instrument in `$RV`/`$RC` to pin down the exact DOM state would be appreciated.

## The current behavior

The main thread never returns to the event loop. We captured the exact location twice, in two different engines:

- **Chrome 149**: a CDP `Debugger.pause` interrupt landed inside the inline `$RV` function of the streamed document (single call frame, anonymous inline script).
- **Safari (macOS 15.7, WebKit)**: `sample` of the WebContent process shows **3664/3664** main-thread samples pinned in one stack:

```
__CFRunLoopDoTimers → WebCore::ThreadTimers → RemoteLayerTreeDrawingArea::updateRendering
→ WebCore::Page::updateRendering
→ WebCore::ScriptedAnimationController::serviceRequestAnimationFrameCallbacks
→ WebCore::JSRequestAnimationFrameCallback::invoke
→ JSC::Interpreter::executeBoundCall          ← the rAF callback is a bound function = $RV.bind(null, $RB)
→ (JIT frames)
→ WebCore::jsNodePrototypeFunction_insertBefore   (3644 / 3664 samples)
→ WebCore::ContainerNode::insertBefore            (2043 / 3664 samples)
```

The bound-function rAF callback matches how `$RC` schedules the batched reveal (`requestAnimationFrame($RV.bind(null,$RB))`), and the hot frame matches `$RV`'s content-move loop:

```js
for (; e.firstChild; ) f.insertBefore(e.firstChild, c);
```

Reproducing in **both Blink and WebKit** rules out a browser engine bug — the loop is a pure DOM-semantics issue in the inline runtime.

<details>
<summary>The runtime captured from our page</summary>

```js
$RV=function(a){$RT=performance.now();for(var b=0;b<a.length;b+=2){var c=a[b],e=a[b+1];
null!==e.parentNode&&e.parentNode.removeChild(e);var f=c.parentNode;if(f){var g=c.previousSibling,h=0;
do{if(c&&8===c.nodeType){var d=c.data;if("/$"===d||"/&"===d)if(0===h)break;else h--;
else"$"!==d&&"$?"!==d&&"$~"!==d&&"$!"!==d&&"&"!==d||h++}d=c.nextSibling;f.removeChild(c);c=d}while(c);
for(;e.firstChild;)f.insertBefore(e.firstChild,c);g.data="$";
g._reactRetry&&requestAnimationFrame(g._reactRetry)}}a.length=0};
$RC=function(a,b){if(b=document.getElementById(b))(a=document.getElementById(a))?
(a.previousSibling.data="$~",$RB.push(a,b),2===$RB.length&&("number"!==typeof $RT?
requestAnimationFrame($RV.bind(null,$RB)):(a=performance.now(),
setTimeout($RV.bind(null,$RB),2300>a&&2E3<a?2300-a:$RT+300-a)))):b.parentNode.removeChild(b)};
```
</details>

### Suspected mechanism (hypothesis)

`for(;e.firstChild;)f.insertBefore(e.firstChild,c)` terminates only if moving `e.firstChild` before `c` actually removes it from `e`. If the reference node `c` (the position where the marker walk stopped) ends up **inside `e`** — or `f === e` — the moved node remains a child of `e` and the child list cycles forever (e.g. `[A,B,c]` → move A before c → `[B,A,c]` → move B → `[A,B,c]` → …). That is an infinite loop with no allocation failure, and every `insertBefore` also queues MutationObserver records for any observers on the page (analytics/chat widgets), which explains the unbounded memory growth we see.

We statically verified the **fully-loaded** document: all 15 `$RC("B:x","S:x")` pairs have well-formed markers (close comment is a sibling of the placeholder, segment div does not contain them). So the pathological state appears to arise **dynamically** — depending on which boundaries get batched into a single `$RV` flush and how earlier reveals mutated the DOM. This matches the intermittency we observe.

## The expected behavior

The batched reveal (`$RV`) completes and returns to the event loop. If a marker walk is corrupted or raced — the reference node ends up inside the fragment being drained, or `f === e` — the runtime should degrade to a broken/failed Suspense boundary rather than hanging the entire page. A defensive fix suggestion: bound the move loop, or verify `!e.contains(c)` before the move, so a corrupted/raced marker degrades to a broken boundary instead of hanging the whole page.

## Environment

- react / react-dom: 19.2.4 (vendored by Next.js 16.2.6, App Router, PPR enabled, `cacheComponents`)
- Also reproduced with the runtime shipped in Next 16.2.10 (byte-identical `$RV`)
- Chrome 149.0.7827.201 (macOS), Safari 18.x / macOS 15.7 — both reproduce
- Page: production PDP with ~15 streamed Suspense boundaries, large DOM (~1,700 nodes SSR), third-party scripts present (MutationObservers active)
- No browser extensions (reproduced in clean profiles and isolated contexts)

author: arnplsrz
title: [DevTools Bug]: Inspect highlight and render-update highlight misaligned when page uses CSS zoom property
text:
### Website or app

Any React app with html { zoom: 0.9; } in global CSS.

### Repro steps

**Repro steps**

1. Add html { zoom: 0.9; } to global CSS.
2. Open React DevTools → Components tab.
3. Hover any element in component tree inspect highlight is shifted from the actual element.
4. Enable "Highlight updates when components render" trigger a re-render same misalignment.

Expected: Overlays align with the element (same as browser native Inspect).

Actual: Overlays are offset. Offset scales with distance from viewport origin larger the further down/right the element is. Factor is 1 - zoom.

---
**Root cause**

Both Highlighter/Overlay.js and TraceUpdates/canvas.js inject position: fixed nodes into the page DOM. In Chromium, CSS zoom on an ancestor scales the coordinate system for position: fixed descendants unlike transform: scale which doesn't. So when body { zoom: 0.9 }:

- getBoundingClientRect() returns viewport-relative px (e.g., top: 450px)
- Overlay sets position: fixed; top: 450px inside the zoomed body
- Chromium renders it at 450 × 0.9 = 405px → 45px off

Fix: accumulate CSS zoom from the target element's ancestor chain in views/utils.js and divide overlay coordinates by it. Both Overlay.js and canvas.js use getNestedBoundingClientRect from that shared file.

Browser native inspector is unaffected because it renders outside the page's CSS coordinate system.

**Related**

#36787 proposes unifying both highlighting systems into one canvas, zoom fix would land there instead if pursued.

title: Bug: ViewTransition fails to animate shared elements inside RTL layouts
text:
When using React's `ViewTransition` component in a Next.js application, shared element transitions do not work if the document or any ancestor element has `dir="rtl"`.

The exact same code works correctly when `dir="ltr"` is used.

As a workaround, wrapping the transition element in an ancestor with `dir="ltr"` restores the expected behavior.

React version:

* react: 19.2.0
* react-dom: 19.2.0
* next: 16.2.9

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a Next.js application using React 19 and enable View Transitions.
2. Set `<html dir="rtl">` in the root layout.
3. Create two pages with a shared `<ViewTransition name="box">`.
4. Navigate between the pages.
5. Observe that no shared element transition occurs.
6. Change `dir="rtl"` to `dir="ltr"` and repeat the navigation.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
export default function RootLayout({
```

Shared element transitions should work regardless of the text direction (`ltr` or `rtl`) applied to the document or ancestor elements.

author: TheAlexLichter
title: Bug: `fetchPriority` is not available in `ReactDOM.preloadModule()`
text:
`ReactDOM.preload()` supports a fetchPriority option, but `ReactDOM.preloadModule()` currently ignores
it, ruling out more granular preload optimization for ESM-based apps.

## Details

Frameworks using native ES modules rely on `modulepreload` to discover client-side JavaScript
during server rendering. By default, these get a high priority in browsers.

When a page emits many JS files, they may compete with render-critical resources.

React already fixes this for bootstrap modules via `fetchPriority="low"` and also It also supports explicit priorities through `ReactDOM.preload()` and `ReactDOM.preinit()` but *not* via `ReactDOM.preloadModule()`.

This would enable the optimization so `@vitejs/plugin-rsc` and others can pass `fetchPriority: 'low'` further down (see https://github.com/vitejs/vite-plugin-react/pull/1264).

## Proposed Addition

Extend `PreloadModuleOptions` with `fetchPriority` and forward this value to the generated link.

```ts
type PreloadModuleOptions = {
  as?: string
  crossOrigin?: string
  integrity?: string
  nonce?: string
  fetchPriority?: 'high' | 'low' | 'auto'
}
```

The same option may also make sense for `ReactDOM.preinitModule()`.

## Alternatives

Developers could:

- Rewrite React’s streamed HTML (exhausting and brittle)
- Emit separate preload hints (risking duplication)
- Avoid early module discovery entirely (not performant)
